1151.event_title: Mumtaz Mahal dies at Burhanpur while on campaign with Shah Jahan
1151.event: Mumtaz Mahal, married to the future Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in 1612, regularly travelled with his entourage on military campaigns rather than staying behind. In 1631, though pregnant, she went with him on his campaign in the Deccan. She died at Burhanpur that June shortly after giving birth, and her body was later carried to Agra, where Shah Jahan raised the Taj Mahal over her tomb.
1151.explanation: Rather than wait at home for news of a safe return, Mumtaz chose to go wherever her husband went, and the separation she dreaded came instead through her own death on the journey.
1151.tie_back: The kural's heroine says that news of a quick return should be told to whoever will still be alive by then; Mumtaz refused to be left behind, and her story shows how a long absence can outlast a life.
1151._accuracy_note: The refusal to be parted and the death before any homecoming match the kural's mood, but here the wife travelled with her husband rather than being left behind, so the fit is partial.

1152.event_title: Fridtjof Nansen leaves his wife and baby daughter for the Fram expedition
1152.event: The explorer Fridtjof Nansen, married to the singer Eva Nansen since 1889, left his home at Lysaker in June 1893 to begin the Fram expedition into the Arctic Ocean. In his published journal he described looking back at his home, seeing his small daughter Liv at an upstairs window, wishing he could turn back, and calling that parting the darkest hour of the whole journey. The voyage took just over three years, and the Fram returned in 1896.
1152.explanation: Nansen's own record shows that, for him, the hardest moment of a dangerous polar voyage was not the ice but the farewell at his own door.
1152.tie_back: The kural says that the shadow of a coming parting turns even the joy of being together into pain, which is the feeling Nansen set down on the day he left his family.
1152._accuracy_note: A well-documented record of the pain of an approaching long separation, though it is the departing husband's view rather than the waiting wife's dread before the departure.

1153.event_title: Douglas Mawson misses his ship and spends an extra year in Antarctica
1153.place: Cape Denison (Main Base), Commonwealth Bay, Antarctica, and Adelaide, Australia
1153.event: Douglas Mawson led the Australasian Antarctic Expedition, leaving his fiancée, Francisca (Paquita) Delprat, behind in Australia. Returning alone from a sledging journey on which his two companions had died, he reached Main Base only about five hours after the relief ship Aurora had sailed, and he was forced to remain in Antarctica for another year. Soon after finally returning, he married Paquita on 31 March 1914.
1153.explanation: However careful the plan, Mawson's promised return slipped by a whole year because of events no one could control.
1153.tie_back: The kural observes that even with a wise and loving partner separation comes at some time, so a promise of no parting or of a fixed return is hard to trust, and Mawson's lost year shows exactly how such a promise can fail.
1153._accuracy_note: A clear, documented case of a planned return being overtaken by circumstance, though the sources do not record Paquita's own doubts or any specific promise Mawson made.

1154.event_title: John Donne writes A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning
1154.event: John Donne's poem A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning, first published in 1633, is a farewell in which the speaker tells his beloved not to grieve at their parting because their love cannot be divided by distance. According to Donne's early biographer Izaak Walton, Donne gave the poem to his wife shortly before setting out on a journey to France in 1611 or 1612.
1154.explanation: The poem is one of the most famous reassurances ever written by a departing lover, telling the one left behind that there is no cause for fear or tears.
1154.tie_back: The kural asks whether any blame falls on the one who trusted the lover who said do not be afraid and then went away, and Donne's poem is that very do-not-fear spoken on the eve of a departure.
1154._accuracy_note: The poem is almost the kural's reassuring words put into verse, but its link to Donne's wife and his 1611-12 journey rests on Walton's account rather than on Donne's own record, and the sources differ on the year.

1155.event_title: Matthew Flinders sails without his new wife and is parted from her for nine years
1155.event: The navigator Matthew Flinders married Ann Chappelle on 17 April 1801, and the couple hoped she could sail with him on HMS Investigator, but the Admiralty disapproved and she was left behind. Flinders departed about three months after the wedding to chart the coast of Australia, and on his way home he was detained on Mauritius. Ann did not see him again for nine years, until he returned to England in 1810, and she endured distress and ill health during his absence.
1155.explanation: A parting that both had hoped to avoid, and that was meant to last for one voyage, stretched to nearly a decade once events took over.
1155.tie_back: The kural pleads that the husband be kept from going, because once he has left, being together again will be hard to come by, and the Flinders' nine years apart show how true that fear could be.
1155._accuracy_note: A strong fit: the couple tried to prevent the parting, could not, and reunion did prove long and hard, though the sources record the Admiralty's refusal rather than Ann's own words.

1156.event_title: Paul Gauguin leaves his wife and children to paint in Tahiti
1156.place: Copenhagen, Denmark, and Tahiti, French Polynesia
1156.event: Paul Gauguin, married to Mette Sophie Gad since the early 1870s, had five children with her, and in 1884 the family moved to Copenhagen to live with her relatives, while Gauguin returned to Paris the next year. In 1891, after a successful sale of his work, he paid a final visit to his family in Copenhagen and then set sail for Tahiti. He and Mette remained apart for the rest of his life, never divorcing and corresponding until 1897.
1156.explanation: Gauguin chose his art over family life, came in person to say goodbye, and then left, and the separation that followed was never repaired.
1156.tie_back: The kural says that a husband hard enough to announce his departure to his wife's face leaves her little reason to hope he will return and be kind, and the Gauguins' lasting separation bears that fear out.
1156._accuracy_note: The documented final visit and permanent separation match the kural's point, but the sources do not record Mette's hopes or how the farewell itself was spoken.

1157.event_title: Queen Victoria wears mourning black for the rest of her life
1157.event: After her husband, Prince Albert, died in 1861 at the age of 42, Queen Victoria sank into depression and wore black for the rest of her reign. She kept to mourning far longer than the customary two years for a widow, and until the late 1860s she rarely appeared in public. Her visible grief was so well known that she became famous as a woman in black, and she was criticised for her long seclusion.
1157.explanation: Victoria's clothing and withdrawal announced her loss to the whole nation every day for forty years, whether she spoke of it or not.
1157.tie_back: The kural says that the bangles slipping from a wasted arm will announce to the whole town that her lord has left her, and Victoria's unending black did the same for the loss of Albert.
1157._accuracy_note: The outward sign that broadcasts private grief to the public is a good parallel, but Albert's separation was by death, not a journey, and mourning dress was chosen rather than an involuntary bodily sign.

1158.event_title: Ovid is banished to Tomis on the Black Sea
1158.event: In 8 CE the Roman emperor Augustus banished the poet Ovid from Rome to Tomis, a town on the far shore of the Black Sea. In exile Ovid wrote the Tristia, or Sorrows, poems that include letters addressed to his wife, along with long letters and poems appealing to be allowed to return to Rome. He was never recalled and died in Tomis in 17 CE.
1158.explanation: Ovid's exile poems became the classic record of a person cut off from home, friends and spouse and forced to live among strangers.
1158.tie_back: The kural ranks living in a town where no one is close to you as painful and parting from one's beloved as more painful still, and Ovid suffered both together in Tomis.
1158._accuracy_note: A strong illustration of both pains the kural names, though Ovid writes as an exile longing for Rome and his wife rather than as a woman parted from her husband.

1159.event_title: Nizami of Ganja writes Layla and Majnun
1159.event: In 1188 the Persian poet Nizami of Ganja, working under a commission from the Shirvanshah court, completed Layla and Majnun as part of his Khamsa, or Quintet. The poem tells of two young lovers in the Arabian desert who are forcibly separated when Layla's father refuses the marriage. Qays, the hero, flees into the desert, where he wanders singing of his love and longing and becomes known as Majnun, the one driven mad by love.
1159.explanation: Nizami's poem became one of the best-known love stories of the Persian and Islamic world, and its central image is a love that burns hotter the farther the lovers are kept apart.
1159.tie_back: The kural says that fire burns only those who touch it, while love burns even those who move away from it, and Majnun, consumed by love far off in the desert, is that idea told as a story.
1159._accuracy_note: The documented event is the writing of a famous poem, not a real separation, so it illustrates the kural's image through literature rather than through lived history.

1160.event_title: Nelson Mandela's prison letters to Winnie Mandela
1160.place: Robben Island and other prisons, South Africa
1160.event: Nelson Mandela was held as a sentenced prisoner from 1962 to 1990, in Pretoria Local, Robben Island, Pollsmoor and Victor Verster prisons. At first he was allowed to write and receive only one 500-word letter every six months, and censors read everything he sent. Among the letters he wrote were letters to his wife, Winnie, in which he professed his love and supported her through her own struggles under apartheid; they were published in 2018 as The Prison Letters of Nelson Mandela.
1160.explanation: For nearly three decades a husband and wife kept their bond alive through a few strictly limited and censored letters.
1160.tie_back: The kural speaks of people who somehow bear what seems unbearable, push back their sorrow and live on through a long separation, and the Mandelas endured such a parting for twenty-seven years.
1160._accuracy_note: A documented example of enduring an extremely long separation, fitting the literal reading; the kural's likely ironic tone (the heroine cannot bear it) is not reflected, and the marriage later ended after Mandela's release.
